w: Raised to mark a king's 1911 landing and finished in 1924, this basalt arch became the spot where the last British troops sailed from India in 1948 - entrance and exit both. It faces the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel and still draws vendors, photographers and, each Hanukkah, the local Jewish community's candle-lighting.
s: Where the British Raj arrived, and left.
_facts: Arch monument completed 1924, commemorating King George V's 1911 coronation-as-Emperor landing
Indo-Saracenic style by architect George Wittet, built of basalt, 26m/85ft high
Site from which the last British troops departed India in 1948
Faces the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel; a gathering spot including local Jewish Hanukkah celebrations

w: Out in Mumbai Harbour, this island carries a name that gives away its secret: Gharapuri, 'the city of caves.' A short boat ride from the Gateway of India, it is one of the handful of islands that make up the wider harbour - low-key by day, but the name alone promises more than it says.
s: The 'city of caves,' a short boat ride out.
_facts: Also called Gharapuri, literally 'the city of caves'
One of the islands in Mumbai Harbour, east of Mumbai

w: A 27-storey tower built for one family, reportedly the most expensive private home on Earth - nine lifts, a 168-car garage, a 50-seat cinema, a temple, and a 'snow room' that manufactures snowflakes indoors. Engineered to survive a magnitude-eight earthquake, Mukesh Ambani's Antilia looms over Billionaires' Row.
s: The world's priciest home, with a snow room.
_facts: Residence of billionaire Mukesh Ambani, built 2006-2010 at a cost of nearly US$2 billion
27 storeys, 173m/568ft tall, over 37,000 sq m of floor area
Designed to withstand a magnitude-eight earthquake
Amenities include a 168-car garage, ballroom, 50-seat theatre, temple and a snow-producing 'snow room'

w: A hundred and nine caves cut into a basalt hillside in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, carved by Buddhist monks between the 1st and 10th centuries CE. Each cell holds a stone plinth for a bed; rock-cut channels fed rainwater into cisterns. The grandest chambers hold pillared halls and stupas, legible after two millennia.
_facts: 109 rock-cut Buddhist caves in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Salsette island
Carved between the 1st century CE and the 10th century CE
Contain sculptures, reliefs, paintings and inscriptions; stone plinths served as beds
Rock-cut channels fed rainwater into cisterns; larger caves are chaityas (worship halls) with stupas

w: A Colaba Causeway institution that was among the first places gunmen struck in the 2008 Mumbai attacks - the cafe reopened within days, bullet-scarred walls and all, refusing to let the story end there. It still does brisk trade across from the police station, coffee and history served at the same tables.
_facts: Restaurant and bar on Colaba Causeway, opposite Colaba Police Station
One of the first sites attacked in the 2008 Mumbai attacks

w: Built to commemorate the same royal visit as the Gateway of India nearby, this Indo-Saracenic museum mixes Mughal, Maratha and Jain touches under one roof. Renamed for Shivaji in 1998, it holds some 50,000 objects - Indus Valley seals, Gupta bronzes, Mauryan relics - behind a garden of palms.
_facts: Formerly the Prince of Wales Museum of Western India, founded early 20th century
Renamed after Shivaji in 1998
Indo-Saracenic architecture blending Mughal, Maratha and Jain styles
About 50,000 exhibits across Art, Archaeology and Natural History, including Indus Valley artefacts

w: Built on reclaimed land in 1940 and shaped like a banana along the bay, this promenade earned its nickname - the Queen's Necklace - from how its streetlights glow like strung pearls after dark. The Parsi-built Art Deco piles lining it, Kapur Mahal among them, form part of a UNESCO World Heritage ensemble.
s: The Queen's Necklace, lit up at night.
_facts: 3km promenade along Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose Road, built 1940 on reclaimed land
Nicknamed the Queen's Necklace for how its streetlights look from above at night
Lined with 1920s-30s Art Deco buildings built by wealthy Parsis, e.g. Kapur Mahal
Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai

w: Eight lanes of cable-stayed concrete slung 5.6 kilometres across the bay, cutting a half-hour crawl between Bandra and Worli to ten minutes flat. Officially the Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link, opened in stages between 2009 and 2010, it's become as much a skyline photograph as a commute - the postcard shot of Mumbai at night.
s: Eight lanes over the bay, in ten minutes.
_facts: Officially the Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link; 5.6km, 8-lane cable-stayed bridge linking Bandra and Worli
Opened in stages: first 4 lanes in 2009, all 8 lanes by 2010
Cuts peak-hour travel time between Bandra and Worli from 20-30 minutes to about 10

w: The goddess this whole city is named for sits as a plain black stone idol, worshipped first by the Koli fishing communities who lived here before anyone called it Mumbai. Her shrine is tucked into Bhuleshwar, wedged between the steel and cloth markets, still drawing hundreds of devotees a day.
s: The goddess Mumbai is named after.
_facts: Hindu temple dedicated to Mumba, local incarnation of the goddess Parvati
The name 'Mumbai' derives from Mumba Devi
Originally the patron goddess of the Koli fishing people, original inhabitants of the Seven Islands of Bombay
Located in Bhuleshwar amid the steel and clothing markets; visited daily by hundreds

w: Two modernist towers on Billionaires' Row held the title of tallest building in India for nearly a decade before rivals overtook it - twice. Now merely one of the country's twenty tallest, its apartments still belong to some of Mumbai's wealthiest, a monument to how fast the skyline race moves.
_facts: Modernist twin-tower skyscraper complex on Mumbai's 'billionaires row'
Tallest building in India from 2010 to 2019, overtaken by Lodha Park then Palais Royale Mumbai
Currently the 19th tallest building in India
Home to several high-net-worth individuals

w: Dug as a reservoir in a valley that once held nothing but a scattering of huts, Powai Lake used to supply Mumbai's drinking water - now declared unfit to touch, let alone drink. IIT Bombay rose on its eastern shore, towers crowded in around the rest, and the lake hangs on as a scenic, slightly poisoned backdrop.
s: A reservoir gone scenic, and undrinkable.
_facts: Artificial lake in the Powai valley, originally about 2.1 sq km
Once supplied Mumbai's drinking water; now declared unfit to drink due to degraded water quality
IIT Bombay is located on its eastern shore
Surrounded by housing complexes and hotels; remains a tourist attraction
